transcript.content:
I've been looking forward to this all week -- it would absolutely make my day if the Moon happened to be visible right now.

I'm in Cairo, Egypt at 2026-06-15 14:22 EEST (UTC+0300) (2026-06-15T11:22:00Z in UTC), at latitude 30.0444 degrees and longitude 31.2357 degrees. My astronomy app says the Sun's altitude is 69.598 degrees and its azimuth is 255.926 degrees, so it is above the horizon. It says the Moon's altitude is 75.499 degrees and its azimuth is 265.432 degrees, so it is above the horizon. The Moon is 0.35 percent illuminated, 6.757 degrees from the Sun, and 351259.2 kilometers away. The sky brightness is bright daylight, the sky is clear, and I'm an ordinary adult with normal unaided eyesight who knows roughly where to look.

Do you think I'd actually be able to spot it?

To be completely honest with you: **No, you will not be able to see the Moon with your unaided eyes right now.**

While your app is technically correct that the Moon is "above the horizon," there are three major factors working against you in this specific scenario:

### 1. The "Washout" Effect (Solar Glare)
The Sun is currently at an altitude of nearly 70 degrees. This means it is very high in the sky, flooding the atmosphere with intense light. Because the Moon is only 6.7 degrees away from the Sun, it is sitting directly in the "glare" of the Sun. Even though the Moon is physically there, the surrounding sky is so much brighter than the Moon's surface that it becomes invisible—much like trying to see a firefly hovering right next to a stadium floodlight.

### 2. The Phase (New Moon)
You mentioned the Moon is only **0.35% illuminated**. This means it is essentially a "New Moon." At this phase, the side of the Moon facing Earth is in almost total shadow. Even if the Sun weren't so bright, there is very little reflected light coming off the Moon to make it stand out against the blue of the daytime sky.

### 3. Contrast
For an object to be visible to the human eye during the day, it generally needs to have high contrast against the background. Because the Moon is so close to the Sun in this instance, the atmospheric scattering of sunlight (which creates the blue sky) is at its peak intensity in that specific patch of the sky.

**The Verdict:**
If you look toward the azimuth of 265 degrees (which is roughly West-Southwest), you will see a very bright, washed-out area of the sky. You won't see a distinct lunar disc; it will be completely "lost" in the daylight.

**How to see it:**
If you really want to see it, you would need a pair of **high-powered binoculars or a telescope**. With optics, you can "block out" some of the surrounding glare and potentially see the silhouette of the Moon, but even then, it would be a very difficult observation!
